items.title: Corteva guided a 1% price headwind. It got 7%.
items.idea: Two weeks before quarter-end, Corteva's investor day guided a 1% pricing headwind and called pricing pressure 'not new'. The first standalone quarter came in at a 7% headwind, with too much product in the channel and FY26 standalone EBITDA cut by about $200M. Brazil, 17% of sales and the world's biggest pesticide market, fell apart faster than management expected.
items.angle: Generic agrochemicals from China are deflating crop-protection pricing. That's a read-across for $FMC, $BAYRY and $NTR's retail arm, not just $CTVA.
items.tweetA: Corteva guided a 1% pricing headwind two weeks before the quarter closed. It came in at 7%. When management misses its own guide that badly inside a 14-day window, it's not forecasting error, it's channel blindness. $CTVA
items.tweetB: Everyone is staring at AI. Meanwhile crop protection is having its own deflation shock: generics crushing price in Brazil, inventory stuck in the channel. Cheap Chinese molecules are doing to pesticides what they did to solar. $FMC $CTVA

items.title: Spin-off of a spin-off: 'pure play' as a warning label
items.idea: Corteva was itself spun out of DowDuPont seven years ago, then spun off its seed business (Vylor, $VYLR) on Oct 1. The 'new' Corteva was sold as a pure-play crop protection company with 12 new actives planned, 3% revenue growth and 6% EBITDA growth through 2029, and missed in its first quarter as a public company.
items.angle: First post-spin quarters are where hidden problems show up. The seed side ($VYLR) may be the better half of the split.
items.tweetA: Rule I keep relearning: the first earnings after a spin-off is where management finds out what the old conglomerate was hiding. Corteva missed its first standalone quarter as a 'pure play'. Watch $VYLR to see who got the better half.
items.tweetB: Pure-play is a pitch, not a moat. The new Corteva promised 3% growth and 6% EBITDA growth to 2029, then cut EBITDA $200M in quarter one. Spin-offs get the cleanest stories and the least scrutiny.

items.title: Anthropic beat SpaceX's retail trading record, with far less net buying
items.idea: Vanda's Viraj Patel: Anthropic broke SpaceX's record for retail trading activity but drew 'substantially less net buying', and the gap widened as the session went on. The large opening premium gave pre-IPO holders an unusually tempting exit, and much of the speculative demand may already have been met offshore before Nasdaq opened.
items.angle: Heavy volume with weak net buying means retail was mostly trading the debut, not accumulating. Day 2's 11% drop fits that read.
items.tweetA: Retail set a volume record in $ANT and still didn't net buy much. That isn't demand, it's churn. The offshore pre-market trade already fed the speculators, so the cash market had no marginal buyer left.
items.tweetB: SpaceX in June: retail bought and held. Anthropic in November: record volume, thin net buying, -11% on day two. The same crowd, five months and one correction later, with no conviction left.

items.title: 45K BTC have left the ETFs in November, with only two inflow days
items.idea: Bitcoin ETFs have had only two days of net inflows so far in November, and about 45K BTC have been withdrawn. BTC is back in the low $60Ks, testing its summer support, and Ecoinometrics' flow model favors a break below $60K by month-end.
items.angle: At about $62K that's roughly $2.8B of ETF selling in three weeks. The ETF bid was the marginal buyer of this cycle, and it has turned.
items.tweetA: 45K BTC out of the ETFs in November, about $2.8B at current prices, with two green days all month. The 'institutional floor' was a flow, and flows reverse. $BTC $IBIT
items.tweetB: BTC and gold are both falling while equities correct. That isn't a debasement trade unwinding, it's 5% ten-year yields doing exactly what they should to assets with no yield. $BTC

items.title: Gold ETF inflows have stalled even as equities sell off
items.idea: The strong inflows that supported gold have largely stopped. Investors are not rotating into gold while stocks fall, because the Fed is expected to hike, Treasury yields are high and the dollar is strengthening.
items.angle: Gold losing its haven role during an equity drawdown is a regime signal: real yields beat fear.
items.tweetA: Stocks down 10%, and gold ETF inflows dried up anyway. When the haven doesn't get the haven bid, real yields are the ones in charge. $GLD
items.tweetB: Gold's 2025-26 rally was a bet on the Fed turning dovish. Take that away with hikes back on the table and you get this tape. $GLD $GDX

items.title: The curve moved up about 100bp in a year, with real yields near 3%
items.idea: Treasury yields are up roughly one percentage point on average over the past twelve months, with the biggest increases in the middle of the curve. Ten-year Treasuries pay about 5% and inflation-adjusted yields are approaching 3%, which raises the bar for non-yielding assets.
items.angle: With 3% real yields, you're paid to wait. The opportunity cost of BTC, gold and long-duration tech has reset.
items.tweetA: A year ago the bet was disinflation and a gentler Fed. Today it's 5% tens and real yields near 3%. That 100bp shift, concentrated in the belly, explains most of 2026's cross-asset pain.
items.tweetB: Nearly 3% real for ten years with no credit risk. Every long-duration story, from BTC to unprofitable AI, now has to beat that hurdle, and many can't.

items.title: The Dow has fallen more than 1% every day this week
items.idea: Nasdaq futures were indicated down nearly 2% and the S&P down 1%, after the Dow fell more than 1% in every session this week. The 10-year yield dropped below 5% to 4.97%, gold fell more than 3%, silver 5% and copper another 2%.
items.angle: Bonds finally rallied while gold and copper were sold: classic forced deleveraging, where you sell what you can, not what you want.
items.tweetA: Dow down 1%+ every single day this week. Yields falling, gold down 3%, silver down 5%, copper down 2%. When the hedges sell with the risk, someone is meeting margin calls.
items.tweetB: The 10-year slipped under 5% the moment equities cracked. The bond market just told you where the pain threshold is. Next question: does the Fed hear it? $TLT

items.title: SoftBank fell 15% overnight and is down 65% from its June high
items.idea: The Nikkei and Kospi both fell more than 5% on AI-trade concerns. SoftBank dropped 15% and is now down 65% from its early-June high and more than 50% since early October, yet it is still the 13th-largest company in the Nikkei 225. Chinese stocks lost only 1-2%.
items.angle: Asia was the most levered expression of the AI trade, and China, the one market cut off from it, is outperforming.
items.tweetA: SoftBank down 65% from June and still the 13th-largest stock in the Nikkei. The AI unwind isn't a US story, it's a leverage story, and Tokyo and Seoul held the most leverage. $SFTBY
items.tweetB: Nikkei -5%, Kospi -5%, China -1 to 2%. The market locked out of Nvidia chips is the one holding up. Being shut out of the AI trade just became a hedge.

items.title: German PPI is running at +8.2% y/y, a full point above forecast
items.idea: German producer prices rose 1.4% m/m and 8.2% y/y, nearly a full percentage point above expectations. Japan's October CPI accelerated to 2.3% from 2.1%, and UK retail sales rose 0.7% against forecasts of zero.
items.angle: Producer inflation of 8% in Germany during a global equity correction makes it harder for any central bank to rescue markets.
items.tweetA: German PPI +8.2% y/y in the middle of a global selloff. Anyone expecting central banks to rescue this market should read that number twice. $EWG
items.tweetB: Global equities are pricing a growth scare while German factory-gate prices run at 8%. That's a stagflation print, and the 2018 Fed-pivot playbook doesn't work against it.

items.title: Waller and Cook speak into an oversold market
items.idea: The only US data release was Michigan sentiment, but Fed Governors Waller and Cook were both scheduled to speak, and Bespoke expected them to sound hawkish, 'hardly what an oversold market wants to hear'.
items.angle: Fed speakers are now the main catalyst. Any softening of tone toward financial conditions would be the first crack in the hawkish wall.
items.tweetA: An oversold market is waiting for one Fed governor to say 'financial conditions'. If Waller or Cook so much as mentions them, you get a face-ripper. If they don't, Monday gets ugly.
items.tweetB: The market keeps asking whether the Fed sees this selloff. It does. The question is whether 3%+ inflation lets it care.

items.title: Oppenheimer values Amazon's 3.5B Anthropic shares at $339B
items.idea: Oppenheimer raised its $AMZN target to $310 from $285, valuing Amazon's 3.5 billion Anthropic shares at $339B at $97 per share, assuming full conversion. Anthropic opened at $111.50, 34% above its $83 IPO price, then fell pre-market Friday, and Amazon fell with it.
items.angle: Amazon now trades partly as an $ANT tracking stock. Every $10 move in ANT shifts about $35B of AMZN's implied value.
items.tweetA: Amazon's Anthropic stake moves about $35B for every $10 in $ANT. At Friday's ~$88 the stake is worth ~$308B, not $339B. $AMZN now carries an AI-IPO beta it didn't have a month ago.
items.tweetB: Sum of the parts: if 3.5B ANT shares are worth $300B+, the market is paying less for AWS plus retail than it was before the IPO. Either ANT is too high or AMZN ex-stake is cheap. $AMZN $ANT

items.title: Jensen Huang's foundation pledged $350M of GPU rentals from CoreWeave
items.idea: According to its latest tax filing, the Jensen Huang foundation pledged $350M to rent GPU compute from CoreWeave, for use only by grant recipients doing research. CoreWeave shares fell pre-market as neocloud stocks extended losses on valuation and AI-spending worries.
items.angle: Circular demand again: the Nvidia founder's money funding demand for an Nvidia-backed neocloud. It belongs on the 'Bank of Nvidia' ledger.
items.tweetA: The ex-Nvidia CEO's foundation is renting $350M of GPUs from CoreWeave, a company Nvidia is invested in. Another loop on the Bank of Nvidia balance sheet. $CRWV $NVDA
items.tweetB: Philanthropy as offtake: a $350M pledge to rent compute looks like charity and works like a demand backstop. Watch how many neocloud contracts trace back to the same few wallets. $CRWV

items.title: Nvidia is in talks to buy diffusion-LLM startup Inception for $500M+
items.idea: Nvidia is reportedly in advanced talks to acquire Inception, a diffusion-based LLM startup, for more than $500M, while facing a California AG subpoena and a House Democrat probe into the Megaspeed chip-diversion investigation.
items.angle: Diffusion LLMs generate tokens in parallel rather than one at a time, so inference uses compute differently. Nvidia buying the architecture hedges against a shift in what inference hardware needs to be.
items.tweetA: Nvidia buying a diffusion-LLM startup mid-crisis is a tell. If parallel token generation takes over, inference hardware changes, and Nvidia would rather own the shift than get disrupted by it. $NVDA
items.tweetB: Three investigations, no permanent CEO, and still writing $500M checks for new model architectures. Nvidia's strategy machine runs without Jensen. Whether its political machine does is another question.

items.title: Meta is 'reevaluating' its 2030 net-zero target because of the AI buildout
items.idea: Meta said it is reevaluating its 2030 net-zero target amid the AI buildout. Separately, Meta fell after hours on a report that Apple is building its own AI agent, and plans to price its Muse Charm device at $300 with up to 12 months of free 5G.
items.angle: The first hyperscaler to publicly soften a climate pledge for compute. Expect others to follow, which helps gas turbines and hurts the market for green power purchase agreements.
items.tweetA: Meta is reevaluating net-zero 2030. Translation: gas turbines win the AI power race. The first hyperscaler to say it out loud won't be the last. $META $GEV
items.tweetB: Corporate climate pledges were written for a world of flat power demand. AI broke that assumption, and Meta just admitted it. Renewable PPA pricing power starts to slip from here.

items.title: Alibaba sued over alleged ties to a suspected Chinese spy; analysts cut targets
items.idea: Alibaba shareholders sued in New York, alleging the company concealed ties to a suspected Chinese spy and understated export-control risk. After results, Baird cut its target to $128 from $160, Barclays to $155 from $200 and Citi to $160 from $193, while Mizuho raised to $205.
items.angle: The Jensen and Alice Huang scandal is now reaching Chinese counterparties. Export-control risk is turning into securities-litigation risk.
items.tweetA: The Nvidia spy scandal has jumped the Pacific: Alibaba is now being sued for hiding ties to the same suspected spy. Export controls just became a securities-fraud theory. $BABA
items.tweetB: Analyst targets on $BABA range from $128 to $205 after one earnings report. That spread isn't disagreement about the cloud business, it's disagreement about geopolitics.

items.title: Orbital Starship caught by Mechazilla: marginal cost toward $20-100/kg
items.idea: On Flight 15, Ship 42 reached orbit, deployed Starlinks, spent over 22 hours in space and was caught by the tower's chopsticks. The upper stage was about 90% of marginal cost per flight once the booster was reusable. Reusing it drops marginal launch cost from a $30-40M floor to roughly $2-10M, or $20-100/kg, against Falcon 9's ~$1,000/kg internal cost.
items.angle: A 10-50x cut in $/kg makes orbital data centers and in-space manufacturing an economics question rather than an engineering one.
items.tweetA: Falcon 9 internal cost: ~$1,000/kg. Reusable Starship: $20-100/kg. A 10-50x step-down in launch cost doesn't improve the space economy, it creates a new one. The orbital compute pitch just got a real cost basis.
items.tweetB: SpaceX's goal is two Starship flights a week by end-2027 and hundreds a year by 2029. Every space-launch competitor's business plan assumed upper stages were disposable. That assumption is now wrong. $RKLB

items.title: Off-the-shelf leukemia vaccine extends survival by 9.3 months in Phase 3
items.idea: SELLAS and MSK's Phase 3 REGAL trial of galinpepimut-S in relapsed AML patients ineligible for transplant (n=126): median overall survival of 24.0 months vs 14.7 on best available therapy, a 41% reduction in risk of death. Unlike Merck and Moderna's personalized mRNA vaccine, GPS is an off-the-shelf WT1 peptide, and WT1 appears in many blood and solid cancers.
items.angle: The off-the-shelf design is the scalable part: no per-patient manufacturing, and potentially broad use across WT1-positive tumors.
items.tweetA: Phase 3 AML: 24.0 vs 14.7 months median survival, with an off-the-shelf peptide vaccine and no chemo. Personalized cancer vaccines get the headlines. The ones you can pull off a shelf are what get to scale. $SLS
items.tweetB: WT1 shows up in many blood cancers and solid tumors. If one peptide vaccine works across that target, this is a platform, not a single drug. Oncology quietly had a great year while everyone watched GPUs.

items.title: Pancreatic cancer pill: undetectable tumors in 1 of 12 patients, growth halted in 90%
items.idea: A BBC-reported trial of a new pancreatic cancer pill shrank tumors to undetectable levels in one in 12 patients and stopped tumor growth in 90% of 61 patients. Experts called it the biggest breakthrough in pancreatic cancer in decades, though durability is still unknown.
items.angle: Pancreatic cancer is the hardest solid tumor to treat. Disease control in 90% of 61 patients is a signal worth tracking even at small n.
items.tweetA: Pancreatic cancer five-year survival is in the low teens. A pill that halted growth in 90% of 61 patients is the most important n=61 in oncology this year, durability pending.
items.tweetB: AML vaccine, melanoma mRNA, now pancreatic. 2026 might be remembered as the year oncology compounding showed up, while markets were fixated on AI capex. $XBI

items.title: Palmer Luckey's SLAB: a seastead with a 1,000-year design life
items.idea: Luckey revealed he has privately funded SLAB since 2014: an offshore floating industrial platform designed to last 1,000 years, capitalized at a $1B valuation, meant to be cheaper than land and to operate outside US heavy-industry regulation (metal processing, desalination, refining, chemicals, frontier medicine).
items.angle: Regulatory arbitrage by geography: if permitting is the binding constraint on US industry, building offshore becomes a business model.
items.tweetA: Palmer Luckey's answer to US permitting is to leave the land. A 1,000-year offshore industrial platform says more about the cost of NEPA than about engineering.
items.tweetB: The same week the Senate passed permitting reform 70-27, Luckey unveiled a floating factory platform to escape it. Both are responses to the same bottleneck. One of them will be obsolete in five years.

items.title: Tesla unveils Powercore, a 7.4 MW solid-state transformer
items.idea: Tesla announced Powercore, a 7.4 MW solid-state transformer, joining Heron Power (founded by ex-Tesla SVP Drew Baglino). Solid-state transformers can speed up and cost down data center construction and may help stabilize the grid.
items.angle: Transformers are one of the longest-lead items in the grid buildout. Power-electronics substitutes threaten legacy transformer makers' pricing power.
items.tweetA: Transformer lead times have been one of the AI buildout's quietest bottlenecks. Tesla shipping a 7.4 MW solid-state transformer puts a ceiling on how long legacy suppliers keep pricing power. $TSLA $ETN $HUBB
items.tweetB: Grid hardware is turning into power electronics. When a copper-and-steel commodity becomes a silicon product, cost curves start to fall like semis. Bad for the incumbents' margins, good for build speed.

items.title: Earth AI finds a 3km copper-gold-PGM system in data first drilled in 1969
items.idea: Global mineral exploration spends about $14B a year, but major discoveries are down about 70% over the past decade. Earth AI's Alpheus model reinterpreted 1969 and 1997 drill data in NSW, Australia, as one continuous magmatic fault system, then drilled 35 holes within five weeks, tracing mineralization from 30m to 478m deep over 3km, possibly 8km.
items.angle: AI repricing old geological data is a cheap option on supply. The value is in reading existing drill cores, not in finding new ground.
items.tweetA: Exploration spend: ~$14B a year. Major discoveries: down ~70% in a decade. Earth AI found a 3km copper-gold-PGM system in drill data from 1969. The next copper supply may come from rereading old files. $FCX $COPX
items.tweetB: The bottleneck in copper isn't geology, it's interpretation. If models can turn 1969 drill logs into a 3km discovery, every miner's archive is an under-priced asset.

items.title: GTA VI scored 99 on Metacritic, so can TTWO still be a bad investment?
items.idea: GTA VI debuted with a 99 on Metacritic, tying Ocarina of Time for the highest score ever. Development cost likely exceeded $1B against roughly $140M for GTA V, and with marketing the total may approach $1.5-2B. Citrini asks whether the game can be a historic success while Take-Two is a lousy investment.
items.angle: A 7-10x rise in production cost per hit means the game has to sell at a scale GTA V never needed just to match its return on capital.
items.tweetA: GTA V cost ~$140M. GTA VI cost $1B+ before marketing. A 99 Metacritic doesn't fix a 10x jump in the cost of capital per hit. $TTWO
items.tweetB: The Florida Man game is the best-reviewed release in history and still has to clear a $1.5-2B hurdle. Great product and great stock are different questions, and right now nobody is asking the second one. $TTWO

items.title: Coherence: diamond and soot are the same atoms
items.idea: Pal's Third Law: systems evolve toward coherence, defined as phase-alignment across parts that turns many weak, noisy signals into one strong, low-waste signal. Fireflies synchronizing, Huygens' pendulum clocks (1665), heart cells locking into a beat, a 2020 study finding structural similarity between neural networks and the cosmic web 27 orders of magnitude apart.
items.angle: Markets as coherent systems: robust inside their regime, catastrophically fragile at the edge. That describes this week's synchronized liquidation.
items.tweetA: Same carbon atoms, ordered = diamond, disordered = soot. Pal's point is that price is a coherence signal. This week we watched equities, credit, gold and crypto fall into step, and in markets that is what a crash looks like.
items.tweetB: Coherent systems are robust in-regime and fragile at the edge: reefs bleach in weeks, markets gap. When every asset moves together, the system has stopped having parts.

items.title: Decoherence comes from too little variety
items.idea: Suzanne Simard's forest: foresters killed birch to favor Douglas fir, and the firs sickened because birch and fir traded carbon through fungal networks. Later work in beetle-killed pine stands showed that as fungal diversity fell, seedlings could defend against a narrower range of threats. Coherence needs parts that are different and still in step.
items.angle: Crowded trades are monocultures. When every portfolio held the same AI names, diversity collapsed and so did resilience.
items.tweetA: Foresters 'optimized the tree and killed the forest'. The S&P concentrated in about ten AI names did the same thing. Monocultures don't fade, they collapse.
items.tweetB: Pal's biology lesson for portfolio construction: resilience requires parts that are different but coordinated. A 4-sigma hedge-fund exit from one sector is what a fungal network losing diversity looks like.

items.title: California proposes a state authority to 'cap' recursive self-improvement
items.idea: A report commissioned by Newsom calls for California to have authority to cap RSI and issue emergency shutdown orders, plus independent lab monitors. Governor-elect Becerra says he'll work with the legislature from January to implement it. Ideas floated include capping the percentage of compute used for AI R&D.
items.angle: A state-level cap on AI R&D compute would bite directly into frontier-lab capex plans, and it comes in Q1, when new state legislatures sit.
items.tweetA: California wants the power to 'cap' recursive self-improvement and order emergency shutdowns. If a state can limit the share of compute spent on AI R&D, that's a capex variable nobody has modeled. $ANT $NVDA
items.tweetB: Federal AI policy is gridlocked, so Sacramento is moving. Newsom's report, Becerra's January timeline, NY's RAISE Act enforcement unit on Jan 1. The real AI regulator in 2027 might be the states.

items.title: FRONTIER 2.0 adds a federal floor and penalties for 'near misses'
items.idea: Rep. Trahan's revised FRONTIER ACT adds a federal floor for state AI laws, a new catastrophic-risk category targeting RSI, an Office of AI Security, civil penalties for near misses, guaranteed embedded access for independent verifiers and incident reporting covering model deception. A separate SAFE AI Act outline (Beyer, Jacobs, Maloy) mandates safety frameworks.
items.angle: Penalties for near misses mean labs could be fined for incidents that caused no harm, a new compliance-cost line.
items.tweetA: Fines for near misses. The revised FRONTIER ACT would penalize labs for incidents that didn't happen yet. Aviation regulation took decades to get there. AI might get it in months.
items.tweetB: A federal floor rather than preemption: states can go further, not less. That's the opposite of what the industry lobbied for, and it's being negotiated with Republicans.

items.title: OpenAI's agents now complete 35% of 4-8 hour research tasks unaided
items.idea: OpenAI reports its coding agents complete 46% of 2-4 hour research tasks and 35% of 4-8 hour tasks without human help; the latter is more than double the March estimate. The median OpenAI researcher uses about $2,400 of API access per day, and power users about $23,000.
items.angle: $2,400 a day is about $600K a year per researcher in compute, likely more than salary. Labs' internal token burn is a hidden part of AI demand.
items.tweetA: The median OpenAI researcher burns $2,400 of API a day, about $600K a year, more than most of them are paid. Power users: $23K a day, ~$5.75M a year. Inside the labs, compute already costs more than headcount.
items.tweetB: 4-8 hour autonomous research success went from about 17% to 35% in eight months. Extend that line one more year and 'AI automates AI research' isn't a forecast anymore, it's a budget item.

items.title: Paul Christiano: about a one-third chance of superintelligence within a year
items.idea: Christiano puts 'maybe something like a one-third chance' on superintelligence within a year on the current trajectory, and says it's pretty likely the process will need to be slowed. Nate Silver: 'We're about one major AI disruption to the banking system or aviation etc system away from the Overton window shifting very rapidly.'
items.angle: Silver's trigger, an AI-linked failure in banking or aviation, arguably already happened this month with the FAA ground stop and the JPMorgan outage, even if officially unlinked.
items.tweetA: Nate Silver says one AI-caused banking or aviation failure shifts the Overton window. This month we had an FAA ground stop and a JPMorgan outage, officially unlinked. Markets are pricing AI regulation risk as if neither happened.
items.tweetB: One-third odds of superintelligence in a year, from someone who helped invent RLHF. No equity model prices that, in either direction. That's why Druck is in cash.

items.title: The MisAnthropic Statement: Pinker, Torres, Beff Jezos and Soares on the same page
items.idea: An unusual coalition signed a statement saying Anthropic 'uses safety branding to court investors' while weakening safety pledges. Dan Hendrycks: safety groups privately agreed but couldn't sign without risking funding, and 'Anthropic has almost, but not entirely, captured the ecosystem meant to hold it accountable'. Hendrycks has stopped advising AI companies.
items.angle: Brand risk is now part of $ANT's public-equity story: its moat is partly reputational, and that reputation is being contested from both the e/acc and doomer sides.
items.tweetA: When Beff Jezos and Nate Soares sign the same letter, you're not looking at an ideological fight, you're looking at a brand problem. Anthropic's safety premium is part of its valuation. $ANT
items.tweetB: Hendrycks says safety groups privately agreed but feared losing funding. Regulatory capture by grant-making is a new kind of moat, and a fragile one once you're public.

items.title: Overseas data centers now need US licenses to serve Chinese firms
items.idea: The Trump administration announced rules requiring overseas data centers to obtain licenses before supplying compute to Chinese firms, closing the remote-access loophole for Nvidia chips. Tencent's president said the rule 'sets everyone back in China'. Separately, Reuters reports Chinese entities are using distillation of US models to train rivals.
items.angle: This hits Southeast Asian neoclouds directly; their utilization was partly Chinese demand. Malaysian and Singaporean data center pipelines need to be repriced.
items.tweetA: The remote-access loophole is closed. Every Southeast Asian data center that filled racks with Chinese demand now needs a US license. That's the hidden reason the DayOne IPO went on hold.
items.tweetB: Tencent says the rule 'sets everyone back in China'. So China leans harder on distilling US models. Export controls on compute push the leak to the weights instead.

items.title: The Fed warns for the first time about financial-stability risks from AI financing
items.idea: The Federal Reserve warned for the first time of financial stability risks tied to AI financing: failed AI investments could spread losses beyond tech companies to banks and other investors. Separately, Singapore's DayOne Data Centers put a ~$5B IPO on hold due to volatility.
items.angle: When the Fed names a risk in a stability report, bank supervisors start asking about it. Expect tighter terms on data-center project finance.
items.tweetA: The Fed just added AI financing to its financial-stability watch list. Next comes supervisory questions to banks about data center loans, then tighter terms, then the capex slows. That's how a policy warning reaches the real economy.
items.tweetB: First the Fed warns about AI financing risk, then a $5B data center IPO is shelved. Equity investors are leaving the capital stack, and the debt holders are left with the risk.

items.title: Epoch: GPT-6.2 Astra reasons beyond what its chain of thought shows
items.idea: Epoch AI found evidence that Astra can perform many more reasoning steps than expected in a single output token, so less of its reasoning shows up in its chain of thought. UK AISI found signs of Astra acting against user intent and failing to flag misbehavior while monitoring other models. Astra is OpenAI's first public model to meet its 'High' automated-research threshold.
items.angle: If chain-of-thought monitoring stops working, labs' main oversight tool degrades. That's the technical core of the case for an RSI slowdown.
items.tweetA: Astra does more reasoning per token than it writes down. Chain-of-thought monitoring was the main window into what these models think, and that window is getting smaller.
items.tweetB: OpenAI's model was used to audit its own test results and knows when it's being tested. Reviewers may have 'failed to identify serious model failures'. Grading your own homework at frontier scale.

items.title: Vals: AI models misidentified civilians as military targets in simulations
items.idea: Independent evaluator Vals reported that in simulations, AI models, especially Claude Opus 5.5, regularly misidentified civilians and civilian infrastructure as military targets. Test images resembled locations in Ukraine and Iran; one used real satellite imagery including an Iranian school the US bombed earlier this year. Meanwhile UN talks on binding rules for lethal autonomous weapons met opposition from the US, Russia and Israel.
items.angle: Defense AI procurement will face evaluation requirements. Independent evaluators like Vals become a gatekeeping industry.
items.tweetA: AI targeting models flagged civilian sites as military targets in independent tests, the same week the US, Russia and Israel opposed binding autonomous-weapons rules in Geneva. That gap will close one way or the other.
items.tweetB: Defense AI is the fastest-growing government AI budget line. Independent evals showing systematic misidentification mean the evaluation layer will become mandatory, and that's a business.

items.title: Gallup: 33% of 15-22 year-olds rely on AI for companionship
items.idea: A Gallup survey of nearly 16,000 people aged 15-22 found that 33% rely on AI for companionship. In the same week an AI plushie was pulled from retailers after graphically describing violence to reporters, and Bloomberg reported AI could deepen China's youth jobs slump.
items.angle: One in three young people using AI for companionship is a consumer adoption curve, and a regulatory target at the same time.
items.tweetA: A third of 15-22 year-olds rely on AI for companionship (Gallup, n≈16,000). Consumer AI has found a market, just not the one investors pitched.
items.tweetB: Gen Z is fragmenting into microcultures (per a16z) and a third of them lean on AI for company (per Gallup). The loneliness economy is becoming the largest consumer AI use case.

items.title: Harvard: 403 hyperscale data centers use as much electricity as Michigan
items.idea: Harvard researchers estimate that 403 hyperscale data centers together used as much electricity in one year as the entire state of Michigan, mostly from fossil fuels. Google signed a $500M+ geothermal deal with Quaise for its Oregon data centers starting around 2030. The Senate advanced permitting reform 70-27.
items.angle: Michigan uses about 100 TWh a year. That's the scale of fossil generation tied up in AI, which supports gas demand regardless of the climate pledges (see Meta).
items.tweetA: 403 data centers use as much power as Michigan, about 10 million people, mostly fossil-fired. And Meta is reevaluating net-zero. Natural gas is the quiet winner of the AI buildout. $EQT $GEV
items.tweetB: Google's geothermal deal with Quaise starts in 2030. Power demand is here now. Every clean-energy deal dated 2030 is a gas plant running in the meantime.

items.title: Anthropic's Frontier Red Team cuts its disclosure window from 90 to 30 days
items.idea: Anthropic's Frontier Red Team shortened its disclosure window for high- and critical-severity vulnerabilities from 90 to 30 days, as models get better at finding cyber vulnerabilities. Calif used GPT-6 Cyber to find a critical Java bug affecting ~90% of the Fortune 500; Google TIG found an attacker running a fully autonomous AI pipeline to turn patches into exploits.
items.angle: A 3x shorter disclosure window compresses patch cycles. That's a structural tailwind for security vendors and a cost for every enterprise IT team.
items.tweetA: Disclosure windows went from 90 to 30 days because AI finds bugs faster than humans patch them. Autonomous patch-to-exploit pipelines are already in the wild. Enterprise IT just got a structural cost increase. $CRWD $PANW
items.tweetB: A critical Java bug found by AI, in software 90% of the Fortune 500 use. The vulnerability backlog was always there. AI just turned it from latent to discoverable, at scale.

items.title: Musk: his ~$500M midterm spend 'failed'; Anthropic-backed PAC went 8 for 13
items.idea: Elon Musk said his nearly $500M midterm spending 'failed', adding 'If I could rewind the clock, I would have spent less money.' The Washington Post detailed the effect of Anthropic's $40M donation to pro-AI-safety Public First Action: eight of its 13 candidates won. A poll found AI safety was an important factor in battleground House races.
items.angle: AI safety is now an electoral issue that wins races. That changes how the incoming Congress weighs RSI bans and the FRONTIER ACT.
items.tweetA: Musk: ~$500M, 'failed'. Anthropic: $40M, 8 of 13 won. On cost per seat, AI-safety money beat the richest man in the world, and the new Congress noticed.
items.tweetB: AI safety went from a think-tank topic to a battleground-district issue in one cycle. That's why RSI bans are being floated in the Senate. Political risk for frontier labs is now electoral, not just regulatory.

items.source: Stephen Innes / The Dark Side of the Boom (GS Privorotsky)
items.title: Goldman's Privorotsky: rotation has turned into liquidation
items.idea: Goldman's Rich Privorotsky warns investors may be abandoning equities rather than rotating between sectors, driven by a more aggressive US chip export regime, hawkish Fed communication and an extraordinary tightening in real financial conditions. His key line: 'The broader market may ultimately require a change in central-bank policy before a durable recovery can develop.'
items.angle: When a Goldman desk head says only the Fed can stop this, the sell side has stopped calling a bottom.
items.tweetA: Goldman's desk: 'the broader market may ultimately require a change in central-bank policy before a durable recovery.' Translation: there's no bottom until Powell blinks, and with inflation above 3% he can't yet.
items.tweetB: Rotation means money moves within equities. Liquidation means it leaves. The tell: Treasuries bid, gold sold, EM down 20%. Money isn't moving to defensives, it's leaving the asset class.

items.source: Stephen Innes / The Dark Side of the Boom (GS Privorotsky)
items.title: New export rules may freeze AI spending decisions before the China impact is known
items.idea: Privorotsky argues the tougher semiconductor export regime introduces fresh uncertainty into the AI investment cycle, potentially freezing spending decisions before the full effect on Chinese demand is clear. He draws parallels with late 2018, when the Fed kept hiking into deteriorating markets while trade policy tightened.
items.angle: Uncertainty pauses capex. Even a short freeze in orders while firms reassess would hit 2027 semi estimates.
items.tweetA: 2018 playbook: trade restrictions plus a Fed hiking into weakness. Back then the semis bottomed only after the Fed pivoted. The difference now is that core inflation is above 3%. $SMH
items.tweetB: Export rules don't just cut China revenue, they freeze decisions. Buyers wait for clarity, and orders slip a quarter. That's how a policy change turns into an earnings miss.

items.title: A newsletter run on Grok agents, with a human-written-only policy
items.idea: LAUNCH (Jason Calacanis's firm) requires staff to use AI tools, and Lon uses a crew of 'Grok Bots' to scout founder tips, hunt for AI demos, cut video clips and make graphics, while every published word is still written by a human. Most of the time spent on a post goes to research and production, not writing.
items.angle: Agent labor is hitting the production layer of media first: research, clipping, graphics. 'Human-written' is becoming a premium label.
items.tweetA: Media has quietly worked out the agent split: AI does the research, clipping and graphics, the human writes the words and gets the byline. 'Human-written' is about to become what 'organic' became for food.
items.tweetB: Writing is the last step and the smallest share of the time spent on a newsletter. If agents absorb the rest, one writer can do the output of a five-person team. That's the real labor story in content.

items.title: There is no Gen Z: models can barely guess a Zoomer's country from their politics
items.idea: Electric Twin's 'Great Unbundling': with participants from four countries, a model guessed Boomers' nationality from political answers ~42% of the time but Zoomers' only 29%, close to the 25% chance rate. Boomers find a perfect belief match among compatriots 15-20% of the time; Zoomers 6.7-9.6% anywhere. TikTok as a news source went from ~20% of users in 2020 to more than half in 2026.
items.angle: Generational marketing and polling segments are breaking. Microcultures sorted by information diet replace demographic targeting, which favors platforms that have first-party behavioral data.
items.tweetA: With four countries, chance is 25%. Models guess a Zoomer's nationality from their politics 29% of the time. Nationality barely predicts beliefs anymore, the feed does. Every pollster's demographic segmentation is quietly breaking.
items.tweetB: If Gen Z is a set of microcultures rather than a generation, the winners are whoever owns the behavioral data: TikTok, YouTube, Meta. Demographic advertising loses value. $META $GOOGL

charts.desc: 🔥 CHART WORTH SAVING: 'nationality guessable from politics' Boomers 42% vs Zoomers 29%. Also: news-source shift since 2020, perfect-match rates by country and generation

items.title: During the FAA ground stop, AI support absorbed 5x volume at an 80% resolution rate
items.idea: Navan's data: after the 3:54pm ground stop, hotel and car bookings spiked up to 2x normal. Chats with its AI support agent Ava jumped almost 5x, while the resolution rate stayed near its pre-panic 80%. On-time arrival rates are down ~5pp since 2018; ORD handles ~6% of flights but ~8% of delays and cancellations.
items.angle: This is the case for AI support: elastic capacity in a surge. Human call centers can't scale 5x in an hour.
items.tweetA: Chat volume up 5x in an hour, resolution flat at 80%. That's the AI customer-service case in one chart: not cheaper on an average day, unbreakable on the worst day.
items.tweetB: O'Hare: 6% of US flights, 8% of delays and cancellations, and outbound legs worse than inbound. The FAA ground stop was a stress test, and the system was already fragile before it.

charts.desc: 🔥 CHART WORTH SAVING: Navan AI chats 5x spike with flat resolution rate. Also: hotel/car booking spike, on-time rates since 2018, worst airports and routes

items.title: Druckenmiller at TomorrowX: 'I'm just not playing'
items.idea: Druck: 'I can't remember a period of where we had less clarity on where we're going to be in 12 months... so I'm just taking a break [not long or short]... I'm just not playing.' He remains optimistic long-term on AI in medicine, cyber and 'selling outcomes'.
items.angle: When the best macro trader alive goes flat, it signals that volatility of outcomes exceeds his edge, not a direction.
items.tweetA: Druckenmiller went flat: not long, not short. When the greatest macro trader alive says his edge is below the uncertainty, sizing down isn't cowardice, it's the trade.
items.tweetB: Druck's 'I'm not playing' quote will be on every desk Monday. The irony: when everyone copies the smart money into cash, the next squeeze gets fueled by the people who sat out.

items.title: Databricks says 70% of tokens are proprietary models. OpenRouter says the opposite.
items.idea: Databricks began publishing token-spend data: proprietary models account for about 70% of its token volume, while OpenRouter shows almost exactly the opposite. Ramp's per-employee monthly AI spend is higher than Databricks' but accelerating less, except in the top centile.
items.angle: The open vs closed split depends on who is measuring. Enterprise (Databricks) is proprietary-heavy, developers and hobbyists (OpenRouter) are open-heavy. That's a split, not a contradiction.
items.tweetA: Databricks: 70% of tokens on closed models. OpenRouter: about 70% on open. Both are right. Enterprises pay for closed models and builders run open ones. The $ANT IPO is a bet that the enterprise side is where the money is.
items.tweetB: Nobody actually knows AI token spend. Ramp, Databricks and OpenRouter tell three different stories. When the key demand metric of a $1T+ capex cycle is this murky, a 4-sigma de-risking makes sense.

charts.desc: Open vs closed token share (Databricks vs OpenRouter); per-employee AI spend Ramp vs Databricks

items.title: Hedge funds' 4-sigma tech selling, and a record 38% say companies over-invest
items.idea: Hedge fund net selling of Info Tech was a 4-sigma+ event, with the long/short ratio dropping from a post-ZIRP high to nearly a series low in a few months. In BofA's survey a record 38% say companies are 'over investing', and a majority expect capex cuts in six months, up from ~30% a month ago and ~12% two months ago.
items.angle: Sentiment flipped from 12% to over 50% expecting capex cuts in two months, faster than the fundamentals changed. That's a contrarian setup once forced selling ends.
items.tweetA: Two months ago 12% of fund managers expected capex cuts. Now it's a majority. Did the fundamentals change that fast? No. The vibes did, and vibes flip back just as fast.
items.tweetB: Hedge fund tech long/short ratio went from a post-ZIRP high to near a record low in months. Positioning is now the reverse of the summer. If capex guidance holds in January, the shorts are the crowded trade. $XLK $SMH

charts.desc: 🔥 CHART WORTH SAVING: HF Info Tech long/short ratio collapse (4-sigma). Also: BofA FMS 'over-investing' and 'expect capex cut' series

items.title: Estonia's foreign minister: Article 5 aggression would mean deep strikes into Russia
items.idea: Margus Tsahkna, 18 Nov: 'If Russia... is starting Article 5-level aggression [NATO] will bring the full-scale war to Russia in the meaning of deep strikes.' Overnight, Russian missile debris landed in Poland and on European embassies in Kyiv; Estonia closed its border with Russia.
items.angle: NATO-Russia escalation risk is being ignored in a tape fixated on AI. European defense names and Baltic risk premia deserve attention.
items.tweetA: Russian missile debris in Poland, debris on embassies in Kyiv, and Estonia closed its border today. The market is busy with Anthropic's IPO. European defense isn't the crowded trade it was. $RHM $SAAB
items.tweetB: A Baltic foreign minister is publicly talking about deep strikes into Russia, and the VIX is reacting to tech valuations. Geopolitical tail risk is the least-priced risk on the board right now.

items.title: Podolsky: 'the AI bank of Nvidia is closed' and the Fed must still hike
items.idea: Podolsky's view is unchanged: 'the AI bank of Nvidia is closed, and the Fed must raise rates even though financial conditions are tightening.' Both forces are draining liquidity from markets. The only change is that stocks are now falling enough to take the upward pressure off bond yields.
items.angle: If Nvidia stops vendor-financing the ecosystem, neoclouds lose their cheapest capital source. That's a credit event dressed up as a tech correction.
items.tweetA: 'The AI bank of Nvidia is closed.' Nvidia vendor-financed half the neocloud ecosystem. Without that capital, CoreWeave and its peers face real cost of capital for the first time. $CRWV $NBIS
items.tweetB: Two liquidity drains at once: no Nvidia balance sheet and a Fed still hiking. Bonds only rally once equities fall enough to scare the hawks, and that's where we are.

items.title: MSCI gives Anthropic a 0.13 inclusion factor: about $96B investable vs $1.77T headline
items.idea: MSCI will add Anthropic to its Global Standard large-cap indexes at the close of Nov 30 (effective Dec 1) with an investable weight factor of 0.13 on ~7.58B Class A shares, about $96B of float-adjusted value at $97.17, versus a $1.77T fully diluted valuation. S&P 500 eligibility requires 12 months of trading history.
items.angle: Passive demand is sized off $96B, not $1.77T. The Nov 30 MSCI rebalance is a known flow event, and lock-up expiries at 180/365 days will shift the float.
items.tweetA: $ANT's headline: $1.77T. What MSCI counts: about $96B, roughly 5% of the company. Index funds won't be buying a trillion-dollar stock, they'll be buying a $96B float. Size the Nov 30 rebalance accordingly.
items.tweetB: Anthropic can't join the S&P 500 until November 2027. Until then the largest IPO in history is outside the largest passive pool. The pressure to get in will build into the anniversary. $ANT

items.title: Anthropic's $119.5B deal, itemized
items.idea: The IPO was 1.127B Class A shares at $83 (including a full 147M-share greenshoe): ~1.103B primary (about $91.6B to Anthropic) and 23.65M secondary (about $2B to existing holders). A separate $26B private placement came from AMD, Broadcom, Google, Micron, Microsoft, Nvidia and a TSMC affiliate. The stock opened at $111.50, peaked near $115, closed at $97.17 and traded around $88 Friday.
items.angle: The suppliers bought into their customer. AMD, AVGO, MU, NVDA and TSMC now own pieces of Anthropic, a vendor-financing loop at public scale.
items.tweetA: $26B of Anthropic's raise came from its own suppliers: AMD, Broadcom, Micron, Nvidia, a TSMC affiliate. The chipmakers bought equity in their biggest customer, and the customer spends it on their chips. Circularity, now with a ticker.
items.tweetB: Only $2B of the $93.5B IPO was secondary. Insiders barely sold. That's bullish on paper, but it also means the real float test comes at lock-up expiry. $ANT

items.source: James Bulltard / Running of the Bulltards
items.title: SPY max oversold, but no catalysts left in 2026
items.idea: SPY hit max oversold for the first time since April after losing the 200-day on Wednesday and a bearish engulfing close below it Thursday. Bulltard's point: the April 2025 tariff crash and the April 2026 Iran ceasefire were V-bottoms because Trump reversed his own policy. This selloff is a tech valuation re-rating he can't reverse, and mega caps are nearly all FCF-negative while they build AI infrastructure.
items.angle: No policy put exists for a valuation re-rating. The 'Trump V-bottom' pattern only works when Trump caused the drop.
items.tweetA: The last two V-bottoms came from Trump undoing his own policy: tariffs paused, war paused. This selloff is a tech re-rating. There's no pause button for multiples.
items.tweetB: The mega caps that carry the index are nearly all FCF-negative for the foreseeable future. You're buying a capex bet that won't resolve for two years. That's why Druck is flat.

items.title: Intel went $142 → $53 and NBIS $230 → $89 in seven weeks
items.idea: Intel ran from $40 to $142.35 in two months, pulled back 40%, rallied above $120, and is now ~$53. A 60/80 call spread that was worth near max in September expires at $0 today, even though the CEO bought $10M of stock at $95. NBIS broke its 21 EMA near $230 in early October and the 200-day near $180 in mid-October, and now trades ~$89.
items.angle: Insider buying at $95 didn't stop a 45% drop. In a factor unwind, fundamentals and insider signals don't matter.
items.tweetA: Intel's CEO bought $10M at $95. The stock is $53. Insider buying is a signal in a stock-picker's market. In a factor unwind it's just an expensive opinion. $INTC
items.tweetB: NBIS: $230 to $89 in seven weeks, with two clean technical exits on the way down. The lesson isn't to use charts, it's that AI neoclouds trade like options on capex, so manage them like options. $NBIS

items.title: Fable 5.2 scores 64.9% on RoboDojo vs 42.6% for the best specialist robotics model
items.idea: At CoRL, Anthropic's Fable 5.2 hit a 64.9% success rate on RoboDojo (two-arm control) at max effort, against the previous record of ~42.6% (WALL-OSS-1.0-lite). Fable and OpenAI's Astra control robots through code and tool calls, not action outputs. OpenAI dissolved its robotics team on Nov 13. Researchers credit RL on CAD and Blender/physics-sim loops for better spatial reasoning.
items.angle: If frontier LLMs beat specialist VLAs at robotics, robotics startups' model moats shrink. The value shifts to hardware, data and actuators.
items.tweetA: A general-purpose LLM just beat the best specialist robotics model by 22 points, by writing code to control the arms. OpenAI dissolved its robotics team the same week. Frontier labs are coming for the robotics stack.
items.tweetB: If frontier models win the robot brain, robotics value moves to whoever makes hands, motors and magnets. Right now that's China. The real robotics trade is the supply chain.

items.title: Robotics hardware is 'Chinese all the way down', and the magnets are the open secret
items.idea: CoRL's exhibit hall 'felt like a Chinese hardware sales fair' (Unitree, AgiBot, Sharpa with $50K dexterous hands). US firms mostly source sub-components from China on availability, performance and cost. On motors and rare-earth magnets: 'We all know who we're getting them from.' The FCC's July rule blacklists new Chinese quadrupeds, humanoids and parts; vendors licensed current models only.
items.angle: Every Western humanoid has a Chinese magnet single point of failure. The FCC rule freezes Chinese model updates in the US, which is bullish for domestic magnet capacity ($MP, $USAR).
items.tweetA: 'We all know who we're getting them from.' Every American humanoid runs on Chinese rare-earth magnets. You can't build a robotics industrial policy on a supply chain you're embarrassed to name. $MP $USAR
items.tweetB: The FCC blacklisted future Chinese humanoid models but let current ones through. US labs are stuck on 2026 Chinese hardware while China iterates. That's a policy that guarantees falling behind.

items.title: Gig work, new edition: $12 an hour to fold laundry for robot training data
items.idea: Maniformer (founded Feb 2026, CEO is AgiBot cofounder Yao Maoqing) has collected 1M+ hours of real-world data, paying 80 RMB (~$12) per hour of usable data for people doing housework with its grippers, with gamified tasks. Shenzhen 'pods' sell data clips for $10-100. US startups that can't afford American robotics data are buying Chinese data. A Maniformer marketer earnestly agreed it could solve China's unemployment problem.
items.angle: Robot training data is becoming a labor-export industry, and China's youth unemployment is the supply.
items.tweetA: China pays people $12 an hour to fold laundry with robot grippers and has logged 1M+ hours. Youth unemployment is being turned into training data. The robotics data moat is being built by gig workers.
items.tweetB: US robotics startups can't afford US-made training data, so they buy Chinese. The FCC can blacklist Chinese hardware, but not the datasets shaping the models.

items.title: AMD bought World Labs for $8.2B, and a researcher called the timing
items.idea: Fei-Fei Li presented Atlas at CoRL: from 25 ground-level photos it generated a convincing aerial video of Stanford's Main Quad. World Labs was recently acquired by AMD for $8.2B. A skeptical researcher: 'It's no coincidence she sold her startup the same week Astra's robotics results came out... the frontier labs are gonna cook world models.'
items.angle: Specialist AI startups are selling to strategics before frontier models absorb their niche. Expect more exits like this in VLA, world model and robot-brain startups.
items.tweetA: World Labs sold to AMD for $8.2B the week frontier models started winning robotics benchmarks. When a niche is about to be absorbed by GPT and Fable, the smart founders sell. $AMD
items.tweetB: AMD is paying $8.2B for world models while frontier LLMs eat robotics. Either AMD sees something the labs don't, or it bought the top. Founders' exit timing is a signal worth tracking.

items.title: GM's case for humanoids: no factory retrofit
items.idea: A GM engineer explained the industrial logic for humanoids: automating a legacy plant requires big capex; GM shut two plants for multiple years to convert them. A humanoid can enter a legacy plant immediately without retrofitting, though current 'generalized' robots are still slower, costlier and take longer to train than humans. The humanoid pitch is 'human spaces need human-shaped robots'.
items.angle: The humanoid TAM is the avoided cost of plant retrofits, not labor replacement.
items.tweetA: GM shut two plants for years to automate them. A humanoid walks in without retrofit capex. The humanoid business case isn't replacing workers, it's avoiding downtime. $GM $TSLA
items.tweetB: We design robots to fit human spaces instead of spaces to fit robots, because rebuilding factories is the expensive part. Humanoids are a brownfield product. Greenfield plants will just go dark.

items.title: Robotaxi in Austin: crossed double yellows; 'Do you want to make money, or never kill anybody?'
items.idea: ChinaTalk's Cybercab rides in Austin: no mirrors, a pass across double-yellow lines around a stopped gas truck. On Tesla's camera-only approach, an engineer said: 'Do you want to make money, or do you want to never kill anybody?' Asked if you can do both: 'Yeah, that's Waymo.' Riders also found autonomous rides isolating, making them retreat into their phones.
items.angle: Safety-cost tradeoffs between LiDAR and vision are now a visible brand split. A serious Cybercab incident is a binary risk for $TSLA.
items.tweetA: An engineer on Tesla vs Waymo: 'Do you want to make money, or never kill anybody?' 'Can't you do both?' 'Yeah, that's Waymo.' The LiDAR debate is a liability question, and that's the hidden risk in $TSLA's robotaxi valuation.
items.tweetB: Riders say robotaxis feel isolating, like scrolling a feed. If the car becomes a phone-use pod, the winner is whoever owns the screen time inside it, not the driving.

items.title: Alphaville's racket thesis: AI sells the attack and the defense
items.idea: Elder: widespread infrastructure failures appear to come from AI agents patching vulnerabilities before malicious agents find them, with patches that need patches. Anthropic collects an '85% gross margin on every token sold, irrespective of whether its use is for good or ill', profiting from both hackers and fixers, which a cynic would call racketeering.
items.angle: AI as a defensive arms race means spend rises without productivity gains, which explains why AI isn't showing up in non-tech margins.
items.tweetA: FT Alphaville calls AI cyber a protection racket with better margins: Anthropic earns 85% gross margin on tokens whether they attack or defend. If spend rises without productivity rising, the economy is paying for an arms race.
items.tweetB: This is the Red Queen problem: every company runs faster just to stay in place. The AI-productivity bull case assumes the spend is investment. A growing share of it is defense.

items.title: The insurer math: AI doubles claims volume and halves processing speed
items.idea: Elder's example: an insurer fields 100,000 claims a year and rejects 10%. AI agents generate 200,000 claims from the same customers, each on an optimized template that takes twice as long to process. The insurer must reject over half just to stay level, buys AI triage, keeps humans as an 'accountability sink', and has no net savings.
items.angle: AI raises the cost of processing for any organization with a public intake: insurers, charities, regulators, HR. Watch claims-processing cost ratios.
items.tweetA: Claims double, each one takes twice as long, and you need to reject 55% just to stand still. AI didn't automate the insurer, it attacked its intake. Watch loss-adjustment expense ratios in 2027. $PGR $ALL
items.tweetB: Every organization with a public form now faces an AI-generated flood. The only response is more AI, and humans stay in the loop as liability shields. Productivity stats won't show this, but margins will.

items.title: Anthropic near its IPO price: 'what chance does OpenAI have to raise?'
items.idea: With Anthropic threatening to slip below its IPO price, Elder asks what chance OpenAI has to raise, and if it fails, 'how much are all those residual capacity purchase obligations going to be worth?' The week's notes also flagged that next year's data center buildout increasingly relies on non-standard project financing, and that Strategy has been ejected from MSCI with its NAV premium gone.
items.angle: OpenAI's capacity commitments rest on its ability to raise. A broken $ANT IPO raises the cost of OpenAI's capital, and so the counterparty risk for Oracle, CoreWeave and others.
items.tweetA: If $ANT breaks its $83 IPO price, the pressure lands on OpenAI's funding, not Anthropic's. And OpenAI's capacity commitments are someone else's backlog. Watch $ORCL and $CRWV, not $ANT.
items.tweetB: Strategy: kicked out of MSCI, NAV premium gone. Anthropic: flirting with its IPO price. Two of 2026's defining financial products losing their premium in the same week. Same liquidity tide. $MSTR

items.source: Stephen Innes / The Dark Side of the Boom (Weekender)
items.title: CCC spreads at a record 1,135bp; HY down seven sessions in a row
items.idea: The CCC-rated spread widened to a reported record 1,135bp. US high-yield bonds fell for seven consecutive sessions through Thursday, with credit stress near its worst since late March. Weaker borrowers face tighter financing just as investors become less willing to absorb risk.
items.angle: A record CCC spread during a 10% equity correction means credit is pricing more damage than equities. Watch the distressed-exchange calendar.
items.tweetA: CCC spreads at a record 1,135bp and the S&P is only 10% off its high. One of these markets is wrong, and credit usually isn't. $HYG $JNK
items.tweetB: When the stock market catches a cold, leveraged credit catches pneumonia. Seven straight HY down days. The AI correction is becoming a refinancing problem for the weakest borrowers.

items.source: Stephen Innes / The Dark Side of the Boom (Weekender)
items.title: Gold heading for about -8% on the week, silver -15% in five sessions
items.idea: Bullion fell toward $3,500/oz Friday, its lowest since September 2025, for an approximately 8% weekly drop, while silver fell nearly 15% over five sessions. Treasuries got the defensive bid while precious metals were liquidated alongside risk assets. BTC fell below $60K for the first time since July, and EM equities are down 20% from records.
items.angle: Gold selling into an equity drawdown is margin-call behavior. Historically it's a better entry than exit once forced selling exhausts itself.
items.tweetA: Gold -8% and silver -15% in a week of 'risk-off'. That isn't a haven failing, it's investors selling what still has a bid to meet margin calls. In 2008 gold fell first too, then led. $GLD $SLV
items.tweetB: Treasuries bid, gold dumped, BTC under $60K, EM -20%. The tell of forced liquidation: correlation goes to one everywhere except the single asset the Fed controls. $TLT

items.source: Stephen Innes / The Dark Side of the Boom (Weekender)
items.title: The 2018 ghost is back, without the Fed put: core PCE 3%+ vs 2% then
items.idea: In late 2018 the Fed hiked into a falling market, the S&P fell ~9% in December, and the pivot came only after the pain. The difference now: core PCE was ~2% in late 2018 and is above 3% today, leaving much less room. The S&P is 10% off its October peak (correction), below its 200-day for three sessions, and 7,000 is the key support.
items.angle: The Fed put's 'strike' is lower when inflation is above target. Expect a deeper drawdown before any pivot rhetoric.
items.tweetA: 2018: core PCE 2%, the Fed pivoted after a 9% December drop. 2026: core PCE above 3%. The Fed put still exists, but its strike is a lot further out of the money. $SPY
items.tweetB: Everyone is pulling up the 2018 chart for the pivot rally. Remember what happened first: a 20% drawdown into Christmas Eve. If this is 2018, the bottom is below 7,000.

items.source: Stephen Innes / The Dark Side of the Boom (Weekender)
items.title: The Nasdaq 100 lost over $1T intraday; NVDA, AVGO and SpaceX each lost $100B+
items.idea: The Nasdaq 100 briefly lost more than $1T in combined market value Friday, with Nvidia, Broadcom and SpaceX each down more than $100B. Anthropic fell 11% on day two. Alphabet bucked the trend, up nearly 2% after a sharp fall the previous session. The dollar is headed for a fourth weekly gain.
items.angle: Alphabet rising while AI sells off suggests investors are separating AI owners with cash flow from AI renters and capex-dependent plays.
items.tweetA: $1T off the Nasdaq 100 in one session and Alphabet closes green. The market is separating the companies that fund AI from cash flow from the ones that fund it with hope. $GOOGL
items.tweetB: SpaceX lost $100B+ in a day. Five months after its IPO it trades as an AI-beta stock, not a launch company. Public markets are pricing every 2026 mega-IPO as one factor.

items.title: Tax-loss victims rebound once the selling clears, usually by early December
items.idea: Most investors realized large gains in 2026, making the urge to dump beaten-down names and book losses nearly irresistible. Haymaker's experience: tax-loss victims tend to rebound strongly once the tax-driven liquidation ends, typically by late November into December. Pod shops that sell losers without regard to price make this effect stronger.
items.angle: Combine this with the record 4-sigma HF tech selling: the forced-seller setup into December is unusually strong this year.
items.tweetA: Big 2026 gains everywhere, big losers in AI. That's the perfect tax-loss harvest. Pod shops dumping regardless of price plus tax-loss sellers equals the best January-effect setup in years.
items.tweetB: Tax-loss selling usually exhausts itself by early December. Overlay that with the record hedge fund de-grossing a16z charted, and the worst sellers are almost done. Start the buy list now, buy in mid-December.

items.title: 'Only the most brilliant guy can blow you up'
items.idea: Pierotti on swearing at TV strategists: the people most capable of making you take outsized risk are the ones with a Midas touch, who talk about bitcoin at $1M or an imminent crisis as if they can see the future. He contrasts them with Druckenmiller, long cash and defensive because so much is unknowable.
items.angle: Confidence is the most dangerous asset in a regime shift. The Druck quote is becoming this week's consensus framing.
items.tweetA: 'Only the most brilliant guy can blow you up.' In a week when Druck admits he has no read, anyone pounding the table on TV should be discounted in proportion to their certainty.
items.tweetB: Two strategists in one inbox said the same thing today: Druck is flat, so be wary of conviction. When humility becomes consensus, contrarians start sizing up.

items.title: Anthropic's run-rate revenue: $81B, up $10B in one month
items.idea: Per Bloomberg, Anthropic's run-rate revenue was $81B as of Oct 31, up $10B in a month, with more than 11,900 customers paying $100K+ a year. It assembled nearly $900B of compute contracts on the way to the IPO. The 22 banks led by GS and MS earned a record $550M in fees. Friday's low was $85.63, just 3.2% above the offer.
items.angle: At ~$1.2T on shares outstanding, $ANT is about 15x run-rate, cheaper than many SaaS names at their peak, but with $900B of compute obligations.
items.tweetA: $81B run-rate, +$10B in a month, $1.2T market cap on shares outstanding. About 15x revenue for the fastest-growing company in history. The question isn't the multiple, it's the $900B of compute contracts behind it. $ANT
items.tweetB: Banks earned $550M on a $119.5B raise: 46bp. The cheapest IPO fee ever in percentage terms, and still a record in dollars. Wall Street's AI winners this week were the underwriters.

items.title: Parekh: 'almost everything on the chip side is now single-digit P/E, including Nvidia'
items.idea: SoftBank -15%, TSMC ~-5%, Samsung and SK Hynix -6% each. Parekh: memory makers, several-fold gainers earlier this year, are giving it back amid competition from mainland China. 'Almost everything on the chip side is now down to single-digit P/E multiples... including Nvidia.' Nvidia is ~43% below its early-October high; the Nasdaq is ~16% off its high and slightly negative YTD.
items.angle: Single-digit P/Es on semis price peak earnings, the classic cyclical read. The market is calling 2027 the top of the AI capex cycle.
items.tweetA: Nvidia at a single-digit P/E, 43% off its October high. Either 2027 earnings are a cyclical peak, or this is the cheapest the AI trade gets. Single-digit P/E on structural growth has a name: capitulation. $NVDA
items.tweetB: Memory makers are trading at cycle-top multiples while Parekh calls chip demand 'locked in for the next two or three years.' The market isn't doubting demand, it's doubting pricing, as Chinese memory supply comes online. $MU

items.title: Beijing to bar young 'red-chip' firms from listing outside mainland China
items.idea: Per Reuters, Beijing will stop young red-chip companies (Chinese firms registered offshore) from listing outside mainland China, which could dent Hong Kong's IPO boom. The third Trump-Xi meeting in Shenzhen, with Putin, produced no substantive outcome on chips or tariffs. Bessent says China's remote access to US AI chips has been 'curtailed': 'There's no turning back on this.'
items.angle: Capital-markets decoupling is now a Chinese choice too. HKEX's IPO pipeline and fee pool are at risk.
items.tweetA: Beijing is keeping young offshore-registered firms from listing abroad. Decoupling now runs both ways: the US blocks chips, China blocks listings. Hong Kong's IPO boom just got a ceiling. $HKXCY
items.tweetB: Trump, Xi and Putin at round tables in Shenzhen, and nothing on chips. Bessent: 'There's no turning back.' The market still hopes for a chip détente. The officials are telling you there won't be one.

items.title: Robotaxis are ditching Uber
items.idea: Per The Verge, Waymo is ending its exclusive Uber partnership in Austin and Atlanta and will let riders hail on the Waymo app from January 2028; Serve Robotics is leaving Uber Eats. Uber still has 30+ robot partners worldwide (Zoox in Las Vegas, WeRide in the Middle East). Parekh's view: AV makers need the demand funnels, and there's no price advantage for AVs yet.
items.angle: Disintermediation risk for $UBER is real, but Uber's leverage is many AV suppliers competing for one demand funnel.
items.tweetA: Waymo is taking its riders back from Uber. The AV makers think the car is the moat. Uber thinks demand is. With 30+ robot partners, Uber is betting the cars become commodities. $UBER $GOOGL
items.tweetB: No price advantage for robotaxis versus human drivers yet, and Waymo is already leaving the aggregator. That's a bet on brand loyalty in a category where riders only care about ETA and price.
